newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China's Dr. Ruth tries to break sex taboos.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China's Dr. Ruth tries to break sex taboos.

text.p: Liu Dalin believes the ancient Chinese philosophers were right about at least one thing - that life boils down to just food and sex.

Liu, aged 64, is now making new career out of meshing China's traditionally conservative attitudes towards sex with the increasingly open and western-influenced views on the subject found amongst young Chinese.

For years, he has hosted phone-in radio shows giving people in Shanghai a chance to discuss problems in marriages and relationships, and also maintains a private museum on ancient Chinese "sexual culture".

The museum, which includes 1,000-year-old dildos and furniture especially designed for love-making, is private because of those conservative attitudes -- officialdom is not wholly happy about his research and activities.
"They don't object, which is progress. But they don't want the topic to get too hot and open," said Liu, who is a professor of sociology at Shanghai University.
DARK CORNER OF CHINA'S PAST
He was prompted to start collecting sexually-related material from China's past by an incident in 1989 when the police asked him to inspect some items they had found.

"They had done a sweep for pornographic material and had found lots of old paintings and books and paraphernalia. Most of it they burned, but they wanted me to give them an opinion of the value of two bags of the stuff they had left," he said.
He was unhappy about the destruction, and decided to gather together the surviving material from this dark corner of China's past.
In ancient China, the study of sex and its impact on life was well developed, if kept hidden. The Taoist religion devoted much time to developing sexual techniques which could prolong life.
"China traditionally was the most advanced place in the world in terms of the study of sex because of its long history and continuity of culture," Liu said.
Liu's museum includes many picture books and porcelain models, many of which fulfilled a similar purpose to the radio phone-in shows of today - spreading knowledge about sex.
There are phallic and female symbols from all ages and parts of China, a wide range of porcelain figures engaged in sexual activity, as well as books and paintings.
DESTRUCTION OF SEX MATERIAL IN CULTURAL REVOLUTION

Liu buys material brought to him from around the country by peasant antique merchants, and has paid up to 30,000 yuan ($3,600) for a single item. He also has a collection of similar material bought outside China which he keeps stored in Taiwan.
"It's difficult to find this material, a lot was destroyed during the Cultural Revolution (of 1966-1976). But there are many antique dealers," he said.
"Initially they didn't dare to sell to me. But I put the word around that I am a professor studying this material legitimately, and it's no problem now," he added.
He pays for his purchases from the royalties of his books on sexual problems, which sell well throughout China.
"This is a transition period, the old ideas on sex are disappearing and being replaced by western concepts," he said. "There is a big difference in attitudes between my generation and young people."
INFLUENCE OF TRADITION OF SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR
"The result is that there is a lot of confusion over sex, and a lot of debate over what is right and what is wrong," he added.

Liu himself, like the world renowned campaigner for healthy sexual attitudes Dr Ruth Westheimer, advocates bringing the whole issue into the open, and stepping up the study of traditional Chinese attitudes and behaviour with regard to sex.
"The influence of tradition on sexual behaviour is very great, so you have to understand China's past to have a clear understanding of what's happening today," he said.
